newsitem.title: UK: Euro products outlook - Supply paints many picture.
newsitem.headline: Euro products outlook - Supply paints many picture.

text.p: European oil products paint many pictures this week, traders said.
Gasoline supply is tightening in the Med, fuel oil is buckling under the weight of its oversupply, and naphtha is teetering on the brink of a dramatic move in either direction.
Naphtha rose about $7 a tonne last week to $227 cif for Northwest Europe, and is $63 or 28 percent above a year ago.
Heavy swaps buying is reluctantly pulling physical prices higher but end-user demand is nearly non-existent and there are fears that an overhang of Med material will end up in NWE.
Four cargoes of 50,000 to 60,000 tonnes will swamp NWE if they cannot be sent to the U.S., traders said.
"We're all desperately looking for outlets outside of Europe because of the margins," a trader with one of the cargoes said.
Gasoline is expected to hold steady to higher versus Brent, after January's arbitrage deals to the U.S. dried up supplies for the first half of February, especially in the Med.
"The arb is still open to the States, freight rates are still expensive and eastern Mediterranean demand is not being met by the Med," said a trader in France.
Lebanon and Turkey are still buyers while the only material available in the Med, from Greece, is too expensive.
"Everything is sold out until February 10," the trader said.
Gas oil prices are seen stable to soft but there is an air of uncertainty over forward price direction.
A bullish sign was speculation a U.S. trade house who was long futures may force a squeeze, but most felt it may liquidate contracts soon, if it did not do so with NYMEX heat expiry on Friday.

They said the trader had managed to take some good profit from keeping premiums artificially high for a while, but the steep backwardation it had created to March gas oil futures was starting to discourage buyers' interest.
"People are becoming worried about having high valued oil, relative to the March screen, in stock," a German importer said.
Traders said much of the key inland market was living on a "hand-to-mouth" basis with good supplies cushioning buyers against last week's $18 a tonne price jump.
"People are saying it's $18 too late to buy now," one ARA barge trader said on Friday.

Russian cargo premiums are expected to remain easy with around eight handy size and four 35,000-tonne plus cargoes scheduled to load at Ventspils in the first decade of February, although traders said some of these may go trans-Atlantic.
In fuel oil, high sulphur is in the doldrums and NWE traders see little room for improvement in the short term.

Poor bunker demand has contributed to a build-up of stored product in the ARA region. Around 400,000 tonnes are in independent storage in ARA and at least two more large cargoes of Venezuelan material are expected to arrive in the next week.

Russian barrels also continue to emerge apace. While total January exports were seen at 500,000-600,000 tonnes, dealers say that current export rates point to at least that much Russian material in February. This over double last year's rate.
Low sulphur fuel oil may be better supported by a little end user interest into the U.K. as well as Italy.
